beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Varun, and this video is about learning from scraps — a classifier built from almost no labels. Every stunning A-I result you've heard about was trained on a mountain of labelled data. We didn't have a mountain. We had three hundred and fifty answered examples — and a disease that hides. So we built a model that could learn from what little we had, and teach itself the rest.

beats.intro_line: Hi, I'm Varun, and this video is about learning from scraps — a classifier built from almost no labels.

beats.narration_text: With few labels, a model learns from patterns. Ours learned from the questions nobody answered — and it worked well enough to build a system on.

props.text:
With few labels, a model learns from answers.
Ours learned from the questions nobody answered.

beats.narration_text: Here's the constraint. Out of our patients, we let the model use only three hundred and fifty labelled scans. The rest, it had to learn from unlabelled. This is semi-supervised learning, and the idea is elegant: a fully-supervised model only learns from answered questions; a semi-supervised model uses the few answers it has as anchors, then studies the shape of all the unanswered data — how scans cluster, which patterns repeat — and bootstraps its understanding across them.

props.caption: 350 labelled scans as anchors; the rest learned unlabelled.

beats.series_slot: BODY ¶2 — the worked analogy + our engine
beats.narration_text: Picture a student given ten worked problems and a thousand blank ones, who mines the blanks for patterns instead of ignoring them. Our specific engine was a design called a pseudo-supervisor: one network learns to detect glaucoma while a second network learns to generate smart training signals from the unlabelled scans — the two improving each other. On top sat a modern vision network, EfficientNet-V-two-S, reading the O-C-T map.

props.caption: EfficientNetV2-S under a semi-supervised pseudo-supervisor framework.

beats.series_slot: BODY ¶3 — THE TAUGHT CONCEPT: why accuracy lies, what AUROC is
beats.narration_text: And how do we know it worked? Not with raw accuracy — accuracy lies. If most patients are healthy, a model that says healthy every time scores high and helps no one. So we use A-U-R-O-C. Take a random healthy eye and a random diseased eye: A-U-R-O-C is the chance the model ranks the diseased one as riskier. Nought point five is a coin flip. One point nought is perfect.

props.caption: AUROC = P(model ranks a diseased eye above a healthy one). Conceptual.

beats.series_slot: BODY ¶4 — the result, and the thing we noticed
beats.narration_text: Our classifier reached about nought point eight five A-U-R-O-C on patients it had never seen — specialist-adjacent, built from scraps. A real result. But it output a single probability per eye. And in that one number, we noticed something everyone else was throwing away.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: if you could only afford to label a third of your data, how would you wring value from the rest? Ask for two concrete methods, and for the specific way each one can go wrong — because a model that teaches itself can just as easily teach itself a mistake. If the answer skips the failure mode, push back.

beats.narration_text: Learning from Scraps. What we noticed was this: the model wasn't just telling us its answer — it was quietly telling us how much to trust it. Next time.
